# XENONnT detector narrows the hunt for dark matter
In the latest analysis from the XENON collaboration, working at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy, researchers carried out a "blind" test to avoid bias in measurements of the XENONnT detector, pushing the experiment's sensitivity to unprecedented levels.

Their results have been published in *Physical Review Letters* and could now tighten the net around several of the leading candidates for the true nature of dark matter.

## Even more subtle signals
For decades, physicists have focused their search for dark matter on WIMPs: heavy hypothetical particles expected to occasionally bump into an atomic nucleus. So far, however, this search has come up short—shifting researchers' attention toward lighter, more elusive candidates like axion-like particles and dark photons.

Hidden beneath the Dolomite Mountains in Italy, the XENONnT detector is built to detect dark matter interactions taking place within a tank containing 5.9 metric tons of liquid xenon.

Normally, this kind of detector would identify particle collisions using two signals: a flash of light and a pulse of freed electrons. But even compared with WIMPs, particles like axions and dark photons would produce only extremely subtle signals—depositing too little energy to produce a detectable flash.

Instead, researchers need to search for the faint bursts of energy released when these particles are absorbed by atomic electrons. Without a detectable light flash, it is much harder for the detector to filter out background noise, such as stray electrons that mimic a real signal.

## Preparing for better experiments
As the team expected, the analysis didn't reveal any unexplained signal in the detector. However, the results set unprecedented limits on the hypothetical properties of axion-like particles and dark photons. The results also edged closer to a more subtle boundary: the point where background signals from the sun's own neutrinos become impossible to distinguish from a genuine dark matter signal. Until now, no dark matter detector had ever pushed past this limit.

The team's results could now set the stage for a new generation of experiments, including a planned successor roughly six times larger than XENONnT, which will require more sophisticated analytical tools to process the data generated in its detection tanks. For now, XENONnT's result stands as the most detailed map yet of where dark matter cannot be found.

# The search for dark matter has been blown wide open
After decades of hunting, physicists still don’t know what makes up most of the universe’s matter. Now they need to cast a wider net.

- Dan Garistoarchive page

June 18, 2026

Underneath an Apennine massif, below the Jinping Mountains of Sichuan, and at the bottom of a South Dakota mine, there is a cosmic hunt afoot.

Isolated deep beneath these rocky shields, massive detectors filled with liquid xenon aim to make the first direct detections of dark matter, the long-sought invisible substance whose gravity has sculpted our universe.

The hope is that someday, a bit of dark matter called a weakly interacting massive particle (a WIMP, for short) will collide with a xenon atom, creating a burst of light and electric charge. After running for years, these experiments have recently begun seeing infrequent blips from a particle that glides ethereally through ordinary matter until it crashes into the detectors. Unfortunately, the new signal is not produced by dark matter.

Instead, the detectors are picking up on something similarly insubstantial but much more mundane: neutrinos, the featherweight subatomic particles that the sun and other stars produce in massive quantities.

> **Physicists’ failure to find dark matter where they thought it was has led to a cornucopia of proposals for new ways to search: quantum sensors, liquid-helium-based detectors, searches in Jupiter’s atmosphere, and more.**

Physicists have known for decades that this neutrino background was there; they were just hoping to discover WIMP dark matter first. Now the chance is looking slim. Some of today’s WIMP detectors are simply so large and sensitive that they are entering the so-called “neutrino fog,” in which the ordinary particles are likely to drown out any signal from the main target. There is no shielding these detectors from neutrinos, which easily slip through the Earth itself.

That means the next experiment to use this long-standing approach for seeking WIMP dark matter may be the last.

Hitting the neutrino fog does not, however, mean an end to the search for dark matter. Researchers just have to shift the focus of their hunt. “We haven’t seen WIMP dark matter,” says Kathryn Zurek, a theoretical particle physicist at the California Institute of Technology. Nor, she says, have scientists found new particles in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the powerful proton-smashing facility that straddles the border between France and Switzerland. “And so people naturally broaden their scope,” Zurek says.

In other words, the hunt is transforming from a narrow probe into a kind of free-for-all. It’s a big shift. Today, particle physicists are less sure about dark matter’s identity than when they began looking for it. They’ll freely admit that they cannot presume the basics—for example, if the stuff that makes up dark matter is heavier than the Earth or lighter than a radio wave, or if dark matter is one kind of particle or a dozen.

The uncertainty can be frustrating, even humbling. “The potential range where the candidates could be is so enormous that the odds of any one small experiment finding it are very, very small,” says Hugh Lippincott, a dark matter experimentalist at the University of California, Santa Barbara.

But physicists’ failure to find dark matter where they thought it was has also led to a cornucopia of proposals for new ways to search: quantum sensors, liquid-helium-based detectors, searches in Jupiter’s atmosphere, and more. “Now there’s a great deal of excitement. And finally, there’s technology there,” says Gray Rybka, a University of Washington physicist who co-leads an experiment looking for axions, an ultra-lightweight dark matter candidate.

content.text:
Most cosmologists agree that something behaves like cold, collisionless matter on large scales. The open question is what that matter actually is. Modified gravity is the only major programme that tries to do without it.

## 1. WIMPs (heavy particles left over from the early universe)
- **Null results.** LZ found no WIMPs heavier than 9 GeV. At 40 GeV, its upper limit on how often a WIMP could hit a nucleus is 2.2×10⁻⁴⁸ cm², about five times stricter than the previous best (LZ Collaboration, Aalbers et al., *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 135, 011802, 2025).
- **The "neutrino fog".** LZ has now detected boron-8 solar neutrinos at 4.5σ (LZ, December 2025, reported by the Penn State LZ group). XENONnT's 2026 light dark matter search found no excess (Aprile et al., *PRL*, 2026). Solar neutrinos are starting to produce signals that look like WIMPs. MIT Technology Review (D. Garisto, "The search for dark matter has been blown wide open", June 2026) suggests the next detector of this type may be the last.
- **Two weak hints:**
  - LZ widened its energy window to about 270 keV and saw one 248 keV nuclear-recoil event in 2.84 tonne-years of data (S. Eriksen, TeVPA 2026, 1 September 2026; arXiv:2609.02823). The team puts the chance that a known background caused it at roughly 0.5% (CNN, 14 September 2026). If it is dark matter, the particle would weigh at least about 200 GeV and interact in a non-minimal way (University of Sheffield via phys.org, 2026). The spokesperson said: "We are not claiming to have seen dark matter" (Al Jazeera, September 2026).
  - Totani reported a gamma-ray excess at about 20 GeV in the Milky Way's halo. It fits annihilation of a particle of roughly 0.5–0.8 TeV, but the rate required exceeds limits from dwarf galaxies (T. Totani, *JCAP* 2025/11/080). An independent reanalysis confirms the excess but still finds a factor of 4–5 tension with the dwarf limits (Stenhouse, Ghag & Deppisch, arXiv:2607.08552, 2026).

## 2. Axions and other ultralight "wave" dark matter
- **Searches have reached the predicted models.** ADMX excluded one benchmark axion model (KSVZ) between 1 and 1.3 GHz at the expected dark matter density. Its spokesperson says the field has moved from instrument development to a "discovery phase" (G. Rybka, ADMX talk, 2026).
- **Candidates are being checked properly.** One haloscope (a microwave-cavity detector) checked a candidate signal near 1.036 GHz and excluded it at close to the DFSZ benchmark sensitivity (*PRL* 137, 021803, July 2026). XENONnT also set record limits on axion-like particles and dark photons (2026).
- **"Fuzzy" dark matter is under pressure.** This is the extremely light end of the range. Lyman-α forest analyses give lower mass limits of about 2×10⁻²⁰ eV (earlier work) or 1.9×10⁻²¹ eV (arXiv:2606.06969, 2026). Both are well above the ~10⁻²² eV that originally made it attractive.

## 3. Self-interacting or more complex dark sectors
These models are partly about what dark matter does rather than what it is. Small-scale lensing anomalies keep them alive:
- A Nature Astronomy paper reports a million-solar-mass dark object that fits neither a cold nor a warm dark matter halo, nor a point mass (*Nat. Astron.* 10, 440–447, 2026).
- A "core-collapse" self-interacting halo fits the compact dark perturber in the lens SDSS J0946+1006. However, it needs a halo of about 10¹¹ solar masses, which ought to contain a visible galaxy, and deeper observations are needed (Li et al., *ApJ* 994, 201, 2025).

These are interesting single objects, not population-level evidence.

## 4. Primordial black holes
- **Candidate signal.** LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA flagged S251112cm on 12 November 2025, a merger in which at least one object appears lighter than the Sun. Its false-alarm rate is only about one per 4–6 years, and no electromagnetic counterpart was found. Theorists call it compelling "if validated" (arXiv:2602.21295; *ApJ* 2026; Vieira et al., arXiv:2603.17009).
- **Constraints.** Most mass ranges are already ruled out (review: arXiv:2601.06024, 2026). The "asteroid-mass" window remains the main place where black holes could make up all of the dark matter (*Phys. Rev. D*, 2026).

## 5. Sterile neutrinos (keV-mass, warm dark matter)
- The main hint was a 3.5 keV X-ray line, interpreted as a 7 keV sterile neutrino decaying. The XRISM collaboration stacked 3.75 megaseconds of observations of 10 galaxy clusters and found no unexplained lines (*ApJL*, 2025).
- X-ray limits already ruled out most of the standard parameter space (*JHEP* 02(2025)213). The programme survives only in non-standard production scenarios.

## 6. Modified gravity (MOND and relativistic versions)
- **Wide binary stars are disputed.** Banik et al. found Newtonian gravity preferred over MOND at 19σ (*MNRAS*, 2024). Chae (2023–25) claims the opposite. Pittordis, Sutherland et al. again find Newtonian gravity fits significantly better, though contamination from triple-star systems still needs work (*Open J. Astrophys.*, 2025). Pasquini et al. found 12 of 26 very wide binaries were hidden close binaries, and the ones without a Newtonian orbit may simply be unbound (*A&A*, 2026).
- **Other tests go against it.** MOND fails to reproduce the observed orbits of long-period comets (Vokrouhlický, Nesvorný & Tremaine, 2024). Galaxy clusters still need unseen mass under MOND. Zhang, Hasani Zonoozi & Kroupa argue stellar remnants supply it (*PRD*, 2026), but that is a minority view.
- **Relativistic versions.** Theories such as AeST (Skordis & Złośnik) can fit the cosmic microwave background, but only by adding a component that behaves much like dark matter.

## Ranking (best to worst shape)
This is my judgement, not a consensus ranking.

1. **Axions / wave dark matter.** They are well motivated by an independent problem in particle physics, much of the parameter space is still open, and sensitivity is improving fast. They have no signal, but nothing has ruled them out.
2. **WIMPs.** The simplest versions are heavily squeezed, and the neutrino fog will soon limit direct searches. Still, WIMPs have the only live hints (the LZ event and the halo excess), mature detectors and a clear path to test those hints.
3. **Self-interacting / complex dark sectors.** Small-scale anomalies support them, but the models are flexible and hard to rule out.
4. **Primordial black holes.** There is one tantalising but low-significance candidate, and only one mass window remains open for all of dark matter.
5. **Sterile neutrinos.** XRISM has removed their main motivating signal, and what remains requires non-standard production.
6. **MOND as a replacement for dark matter.** It still describes individual galaxies well. But clusters and the cosmic microwave background effectively require dark matter anyway, and the solar-system and most wide-binary tests go against it.
